title: Ethylene–isobutane to n-octane
summary: A simplified Aspen Plus V11 flowsheet with a stoichiometric reactor, flash separation, a distillation column and a recycle-and-purge loop, plus a reactor-temperature sensitivity study.
content:
I built this model to practise how separate pieces of equipment behave together in a plant. Fresh ethylene (100 kmol/h) and isobutane (50 kmol/h) are mixed with the recycle stream, heated, and sent to an RStoic reactor operating at 10 bar. The reactor effluent is cooled and flashed at 20 °C and 10 bar. The liquid goes to a 15-stage RadFrac column (feed on stage 3); the overhead is split 95% recycle and 5% purge, and the bottoms is the n-octane product.

The reaction is the simplified stoichiometry 2 C2H4 + C4H10 → C8H18, with an ethylene conversion of 80% specified in the reactor block. Property method: Peng–Robinson.

I then ran the reactor outlet temperature at 60, 80, 100, 120 and 140 °C and compared octane flow, flash flows, and the cooler and reboiler duties. Use the interactive explorer to move through the cases.
results: n-octane component flow stays at about 49.74 kmol/h in all five cases.
n-octane mole purity is about 0.9977 in every case.
Cooler duty grows from −93 kW at 60 °C to −523 kW at 140 °C (more heat removed as the outlet gets hotter).
Flash vapour (about 9.84 kmol/h) and liquid (about 70.29 kmol/h) barely change.
Reboiler duty stays near 1192.7 kW, heater near 514.7 kW and condenser near −233.65 kW.
limitations: The reactor uses a specified 80% conversion, not temperature-dependent kinetics, so this study shows how the simulated process responds, not how temperature affects the real reaction. The reaction is a simplified representation that has not been validated against experimental data. Results also depend on the property method, recycle configuration and separation specifications.
